title: The brainstem: crossed signs and the rule of four
description: Why crossed signs mean the brainstem, how the rule of four turns its anatomy into arithmetic, and what changes when the lesion is a child's tumour.
why: The brainstem announces itself with crossed signs; the rule of four turns a maze into arithmetic.
objectives: Recognise a crossed pattern and use the cranial nerve to name the side and the level.
Apply the rule of four to predict the findings of a medial or lateral lesion at each level, and name its exceptions.
Decode the classic brainstem syndromes as combinations of structures.
Use eye movements and nystagmus to separate hemispheric, brainstem and peripheral causes, and judge a child's sixth-nerve palsy by its company.

sections.title: Crossed findings: the brainstem signs its name
sections.content:
Most lesions in the nervous system are polite enough to keep everything on one side. A capsular stroke weakens the opposite face, arm and leg together; a cord lesion leaves the face alone entirely. The brainstem is different, and the difference is its fingerprint. Here the cranial nerve nuclei sit side by side with long tracts that have not yet finished their journey: the corticospinal tract crosses only at the bottom of the medulla, so through most of the brainstem it is still serving the **opposite** body. A single small lesion can therefore catch a cranial nerve on its **own side** and the limbs on the **other**. Brazis calls this an alternating hemiplegia and makes the rule plain: crossed signs, cranial nerve on one side and body on the other, point to the brainstem (Brazis 2011, p. 12).

**Two facts in one sign**

A crossed pattern answers two questions at once. The cranial nerve tells you the **side**, because a cranial nerve nucleus or fascicle serves its own side of the head. Its **number** tells you the **level**, because the nuclei are stacked in order: the third at the midbrain, the sixth and seventh in the pons, the twelfth in the medulla. The limb signs then tell you how far toward the front or the middle the lesion reaches. Pearl's account of facial sensation shows the same logic on the sensory side: a brainstem lesion numbs pinprick on the face of its own side, because the descending trigeminal tract has not crossed, and often numbs the body on the other side as well (Pearl 2014, p. 47).

**At the bedside**

When a weak arm and leg arrive with a cranial nerve finding, ask which side the cranial nerve is on before you ask anything else. If the face and limbs are on the same side, the lesion is above the facial nucleus, in the hemisphere or upper pons (Brazis 2011, p. 11). If they are on opposite sides, you are in the brainstem, and the cranial nerve gives you the floor. The [[m01-where-before-what|first module]] called this finding powerful because a single observation removes ten of the eleven levels.

In a child the reasoning is identical, but the causes differ: tumours, demyelination and inflammation are more common than the vascular syndromes that fill the adult textbooks.
keyPoints: Crossed signs, a cranial nerve on one side and the limbs on the other, point to the brainstem (Brazis 2011, p. 12).
The cranial nerve finding is on the side of the lesion; its number gives the level.
The corticospinal tract crosses only at the bottom of the medulla, so above that it serves the opposite body.
Face and limbs weak on the same side place the lesion above the facial nucleus, not in the lower brainstem.

question.question: A 9-year-old has weakness of the whole left side of the face, forehead included, and a weak right arm and leg with a brisk right knee jerk. Where is the lesion?
options: The right internal capsule
The right cerebral cortex
The left pons
The cervical spinal cord on the left
question.explanation: Forehead involvement makes the facial weakness lower motor neuron type: the facial nucleus or its fascicle on the left. The right-sided limb weakness with a brisk reflex is upper motor neuron and opposite. Opposite-side cranial nerve and limbs is a crossed pattern, and the seventh nerve lives in the pons, so the left pons explains everything. A right capsular or right cortical lesion would weaken the left face and the left limbs together, and would spare the forehead. The cord has no cranial nerves, so it cannot explain the facial palsy at all.

sections.title: The rule of four
sections.content:
The brainstem looks like a maze of nuclei and tracts with nineteenth-century names. Peter Gates offered a way to turn the maze into arithmetic, and it is worth learning precisely because it is a simplification ([Gates 2005](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15836511/); [Gates 2011](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21551111/)). It asks you to remember four sets of four.

**Four medial structures, all beginning with M**

- **M**otor pathway: the corticospinal tract. Damage weakens the **opposite** arm and leg.
- **M**edial lemniscus: vibration and position sense from the **opposite** body.
- **M**edial longitudinal fasciculus: damage gives an internuclear ophthalmoplegia on the **same** side.
- **M**otor nucleus and nerve: the cranial nerves whose numbers divide evenly into 12 (3 and 4, 6, 12), on the **same** side.

**Four lateral structures, all beginning with S**

- **S**pinocerebellar pathways: ataxia of the **same** arm and leg.
- **S**pinothalamic tract: pain and temperature lost on the **opposite** body.
- **S**ensory nucleus of the fifth nerve: pain and temperature lost on the **same** side of the face.
- **S**ympathetic pathway: a Horner syndrome on the **same** side.

**Four cranial nerves at each level**

The medulla holds 9 to 12, the pons 5 to 8, and the four above the pons are 1 to 4, of which 3 and 4 sit in the midbrain. The nerves that do not divide into 12 (5, 7, 9 and 11, plus 8) are lateral. So a medial lesion names its level by 3, 6 or 12, and a lateral lesion by 5, 7 and 8 in the pons or 9 and 10 in the medulla. Use the figure above to place a lesion at each level, medial and lateral, and watch the findings assemble themselves.

**Where the rule bends**

A good heuristic tells you where it fails. The fourth nerve has a medial midbrain nucleus, but its fibres cross before they leave, so a nuclear lesion weakens the **opposite** superior oblique. The facial fascicle loops around the sixth nucleus, so ventral pontine lesions often take the face with them. The vestibular nuclei lie laterally where pons meets medulla, so a lateral medullary lesion usually brings vertigo and nystagmus. And although the rule places the eleventh nerve in the lateral medulla, a lateral medullary stroke rarely weakens the shoulder shrug. Real lesions, especially tumours in children, also ignore a tidy medial and lateral line. The rule tells you what to look for; the patient tells you what is there.
keyPoints: Medial: motor pathway, medial lemniscus, medial longitudinal fasciculus, motor cranial nerves 3, 4, 6 and 12.
Lateral: spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, sensory nucleus of 5, sympathetic; cranial nerves 5, 7, 8 in the pons and 9, 10, 11 in the medulla, though 11 is rarely affected in practice.
Long-tract signs are opposite (motor, lemniscus, spinothalamic); everything else is on the side of the lesion.
The rule is a heuristic (Gates 2005): the fourth nerve crosses, the facial fascicle strays medially, and vertigo comes with lateral medullary lesions.

question.question: A teenager has a right-sided lesion in the lateral pons. Using the rule of four, which combination do you expect?
options: Right facial weakness and numbness with right ataxia and Horner syndrome, plus loss of pain and temperature on the left body
Right sixth-nerve palsy with left hemiparesis and left loss of position sense
Left facial numbness, left Horner syndrome and right body numbness
Right third-nerve palsy with left hemiparesis
question.explanation: A lateral pontine lesion takes the lateral pontine cranial nerves (5, 7 and 8) and the four lateral S structures. Everything is on the side of the lesion except the spinothalamic loss on the body, which is opposite. A sixth-nerve palsy with opposite hemiparesis and lemniscal loss is the medial pontine pattern, not the lateral one. Putting the face and Horner syndrome on the left reverses sides: those structures are uncrossed at this level. A third-nerve palsy with opposite hemiparesis belongs to the medial midbrain.

sections.title: Named syndromes as worked examples
sections.content:
Eponyms have a bad reputation, and they deserve some of it: a name tells you who described a patient, not where the lesion is. But each classic brainstem syndrome is also a worked example of the rule of four, and decoding them is good practice. Read each one as a lesion, not as a name.

| Syndrome | Where | Same side | Opposite side |
|---|---|---|---|
| Weber | Ventral midbrain, cerebral peduncle | Third-nerve palsy, with a dilated pupil | Hemiparesis including the lower face |
| Benedikt | Midbrain tegmentum through the red nucleus | Third-nerve palsy | Hemiparesis, with tremor and ataxia |
| Millard-Gubler | Ventral pons | Sixth- and seventh-nerve palsies | Hemiparesis |
| Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) | Lateral medulla | Face numb to pin, ataxia, Horner syndrome, hoarseness and difficulty swallowing, vertigo and nystagmus | Body numb to pain and temperature |
| Medial medullary (Dejerine) | Medial medulla | Tongue weakness | Hemiparesis and loss of position sense |

Sources: Pearl 2014, pp. 109-112; Brazis 2011, pp. 393, 397.

**Decoding Weber and Benedikt**

Weber is the medial midbrain in its simplest form: the third-nerve fascicle and the corticospinal tract in the peduncle, side by side. Brazis notes that the third-nerve palsy includes the pupil, because the parasympathetic fibres travel with it (Brazis 2011, p. 397). Move the lesion back into the tegmentum and it crosses the red nucleus, through which the cerebellar outflow passes on its way to the thalamus; now the opposite limbs shake as well (Pearl 2014, p. 110).

**Decoding Wallenberg**

The lateral medulla is the purest test of the S structures. Every one of them is present: same-side face numbness from the spinal trigeminal tract, same-side ataxia, same-side Horner syndrome, opposite body numbness. Add the nucleus ambiguus (hoarseness, poor swallow) and the vestibular nuclei (vertigo, nausea, vomiting), and the syndrome is complete. Notice what is missing: weakness. The corticospinal tract is medial, so a purely lateral lesion spares strength (Pearl 2014, p. 111).

**Why it matters for children**

Classic vascular syndromes are uncommon in childhood, but the decoding skill is not. A child with a pontine tumour or a demyelinating plaque rarely reads like a textbook table; it presents fragments. Knowing the full pattern lets you recognise the fragment, and predict which neighbouring signs to look for next.
keyPoints: Read an eponym as a lesion: which structures, which side, which level.
Weber is medial midbrain: same-side third nerve with pupil, opposite hemiparesis (Brazis 2011, p. 397).
Wallenberg is lateral medulla: same-side face numbness, ataxia, Horner, vertigo and nystagmus; opposite body numbness; no weakness.
Medial medullary: same-side tongue weakness, opposite hemiparesis and loss of position sense (Pearl 2014, p. 112).

question.question: A 16-year-old develops vertigo and vomiting, a hoarse voice, numbness to pin on the left face and right body, a small left pupil with slight ptosis, and clumsiness of the left arm. Strength is normal. Where is the lesion, and which finding most argues against it being medial?
options: Right lateral pons; the vertigo argues against medial
Left medial medulla; the hoarse voice argues against lateral
Left midbrain tegmentum; the Horner syndrome argues against medial
Left lateral medulla; normal strength argues against medial
question.explanation: Same-side face numbness, Horner syndrome and ataxia, opposite body numbness, and hoarseness from the nucleus ambiguus are the lateral medullary syndrome, on the left. Normal strength is the clue that the lesion is lateral: the corticospinal tract runs medially and would be caught by a medial lesion. A right lateral pontine lesion would put the facial and Horner signs on the right. A medial medullary lesion would weaken the tongue and opposite limbs, which this teenager does not have. The midbrain has no ninth or tenth nerve to explain the hoarse voice.

sections.title: The eyes as a brainstem map
sections.content:
The eye movement circuits run the full length of the brainstem, from the frontal eye fields down to the vestibular nuclei at the pontomedullary junction, so the eyes are among the most sensitive brainstem instruments you have. Three findings are worth knowing cold.

**Internuclear ophthalmoplegia**

The medial longitudinal fasciculus links the sixth nucleus on one side to the third nucleus on the other, so that both eyes turn together. Cut it and, on looking away from the lesion, the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct while the abducting eye jerks with nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 45). It is one of the four medial structures of the rule of four, and a precise localizer: the failing eye names the side.

**Which way the eyes look**

A destructive lesion of one frontal eye field leaves the other unopposed, so the eyes deviate **toward** a hemispheric lesion and away from the hemiparesis. A pontine lesion destroys the horizontal gaze centre beside the sixth nucleus, so the eyes deviate **away** from it, toward the hemiparesis (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 148). A seizure reverses the hemispheric rule by exciting the eye field, driving the eyes away from the focus (Pearl 2014, p. 9). A doll's-eye manoeuvre separates the two: it overcomes a cortical gaze preference but not a pontine gaze palsy, because in the pons the centre itself is gone (Pearl 2014, p. 45).

**Central or peripheral nystagmus**

The owner's teaching, which agrees with Pearl's table, gives the pearls:

- Peripheral (labyrinth) nystagmus beats in one direction, is suppressed when the patient fixates, and often has a torsional part.
- Nystagmus that changes direction with gaze is central.
- Pure vertical nystagmus is central.
- Acquired pendular nystagmus is usually central.
- Central nystagmus keeps company: other brainstem or cerebellar signs ("everything in neurology is based on the company you keep", Pearl 2014, p. 121).

Pearl adds a caution: antiseizure drugs can produce a central-looking nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 121), which matters in children on treatment for epilepsy.

**In a child**

Children rarely describe diplopia; they close one eye, tilt the head, or turn the face. Watch the head posture before you test the eyes, and test pursuit with a toy rather than a finger.
keyPoints: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: the eye on the side of the lesion fails to adduct; the other eye has abducting nystagmus (Pearl 2014, p. 45).
Eyes look toward a destructive hemispheric lesion and away from a pontine one (Pearl 2014, pp. 43, 148); a seizure drives them away from the focus.
Doll's eyes overcome a cortical gaze preference but not a pontine gaze palsy.
Direction-changing, pure vertical or fixation-resistant nystagmus is central; check the company it keeps.

question.question: A 12-year-old with a left hemiparesis has both eyes deviated to the right. On a doll's-eye manoeuvre the eyes move fully to the left. Where is the lesion?
options: The left pons
The right hemisphere
The left frontal lobe, during a seizure
The right medial longitudinal fasciculus
question.explanation: Eyes deviated toward the right with a left hemiparesis means the eyes look toward the lesion and away from the weak side, which is the pattern of a destructive right hemispheric lesion. The doll's eyes confirm it: a cortical gaze preference can be overcome because the brainstem gaze centre is intact. A left pontine lesion would push the eyes to the right too, but its gaze palsy cannot be overcome with doll's eyes and the hemiparesis would be on the right. A left frontal seizure drives the eyes to the right, but would not explain a fixed left hemiparesis with full doll's eyes as well as a destructive right lesion does. An internuclear ophthalmoplegia gives failure of adduction of one eye, not conjugate deviation.

sections.title: The child's brainstem
sections.content:
In adults, brainstem localization is taught through strokes. In children it is taught through tumours, malformations and inflammation, and the localizing logic has to work with lesions that grow, infiltrate and compress rather than respect an arterial territory.

**The posterior fossa**

Primary posterior fossa tumours are common in children, and Pearl names the two that dominate: medulloblastoma and the cystic cerebellar astrocytoma (Pearl 2014, p. 63). Medulloblastoma tends to begin in the caudal vermis, giving staggering gait and truncal imbalance with little limb ataxia at first; Brazis estimates it at about 20% of pediatric brain tumours (Brazis 2011, p. 412). As it grows it blocks the fourth ventricle, and the presenting picture becomes raised intracranial pressure: morning headache, vomiting, and papilloedema.

**A new sixth-nerve palsy**

The sixth nerve has a long course across the base of the skull, which makes it vulnerable to raised pressure anywhere, above or below the tentorium. An abducens palsy can therefore be an early sign of a tumour, hydrocephalus or idiopathic intracranial hypertension rather than a lesion of the nerve itself (Pearl 2014, p. 43). This is the classic false localizing sign, and the rule of four helps you decide whether to believe it. Ask what keeps it company:

- **Papilloedema and nothing else**: think raised pressure; the sixth nerve is a messenger, not the address.
- **A facial palsy on the same side, a gaze palsy, ataxia or long-tract signs**: think of a lesion in the pons itself, because a single lesion there would catch the sixth nucleus, the facial fascicle that loops round it, and the tracts beside them.

**Infiltrating pontine tumours and the Chiari malformation**

A tumour that infiltrates the pons does not stay medial or lateral; it gathers cranial nerves and long tracts as it grows, which is exactly the accumulation the rule of four predicts. A Chiari malformation compresses the lower brainstem and cerebellum from below and can be associated with a syrinx, so look for lower cranial nerve signs and for a cape of lost pain sensation from the [[m06-spinal-cord|spinal cord module]].

**What to examine**

When a child presents with any brainstem sign: look at the optic discs, test every cranial nerve including the palate and tongue, watch the gait and tandem walk, and check the reflexes and plantars on both sides. Then decide how urgent the scan is.
keyPoints: Posterior fossa tumours are common in children: medulloblastoma and cystic cerebellar astrocytoma (Pearl 2014, p. 63).
A sixth-nerve palsy can be a false localizing sign of raised intracranial pressure (Pearl 2014, p. 43).
Judge a sixth-nerve palsy by its company: papilloedema alone suggests pressure; facial palsy, gaze palsy or long tracts suggest the pons.
Infiltrating pontine tumours gather cranial nerves and long tracts, as the rule of four predicts.

question.question: A 6-year-old has two weeks of morning headaches and vomiting and now turns her face to the right to read. She has a right sixth-nerve palsy and papilloedema. Facial movement, strength, reflexes and gait are normal. What is the best interpretation?
options: A lesion of the right pontine tegmentum until proved otherwise
Raised intracranial pressure, with the sixth-nerve palsy as a false localizing sign; image the brain urgently
A benign isolated sixth-nerve palsy after a viral illness; review in a month
A right medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion
question.explanation: Headache, vomiting and papilloedema mean raised intracranial pressure, and the sixth nerve is the cranial nerve most vulnerable to it because of its long course. With no facial palsy, gaze palsy, ataxia or long-tract signs keeping it company, the palsy is better read as a messenger of pressure than as the address of the lesion, and the cause needs urgent imaging. A pontine tegmental lesion would usually bring the facial fascicle or the gaze centre with it. Calling it benign ignores the papilloedema. A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion causes failure of adduction, not abduction.

quiz.question: A 14-year-old has a right lower motor neuron facial palsy, cannot abduct the right eye, and has a left hemiparesis. Where is the lesion?
options: Left internal capsule
Right ventral pons
Right lateral medulla
Left ventral midbrain
quiz.explanation: A same-side sixth- and seventh-nerve palsy with an opposite hemiparesis is the ventral pontine (Millard-Gubler) pattern: the corticospinal tract in the basis pontis, the sixth fascicle, and the facial fascicle that loops round the sixth nucleus. The rule of four calls the seventh lateral, but this is its stated exception. A left capsular lesion would weaken the right limbs and spare the forehead. A lateral medullary lesion causes no weakness and involves nerves 9 and 10, not 6 and 7. A midbrain lesion would give a third-nerve palsy.

quiz.question: On protrusion the tongue deviates to the left. The right arm and leg are weak, and vibration and position sense are lost in the right limbs. Pain sensation and the face are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: Right medial medulla
Left lateral medulla
Left internal capsule
Left medial medulla
quiz.explanation: The tongue deviates toward the weak side, so the left hypoglossal nucleus or nerve is involved; the right hemiparesis and right lemniscal loss come from the corticospinal tract and medial lemniscus, both medial and both serving the opposite body. Twelve, motor pathway and lemniscus together are the medial medullary (Dejerine) syndrome on the left. A right medial medullary lesion would push the tongue to the right. A lateral medullary lesion spares strength. A capsular lesion cannot weaken the tongue on one side and the limbs on the other in this way.

quiz.question: On looking to the left, a teenager's right eye does not cross the midline while the left eye abducts with nystagmus. Convergence is normal. Which structure is damaged?
options: The left sixth-nerve nucleus
The right third nerve
The left frontal eye field
The right medial longitudinal fasciculus
quiz.explanation: Failure of adduction of the right eye on leftward gaze, with abducting nystagmus of the left eye, is a right internuclear ophthalmoplegia: the right medial longitudinal fasciculus carries the signal from the left sixth nucleus up to the right third nucleus. Normal convergence shows the third nerve itself works, which excludes a right third-nerve palsy. A left sixth-nucleus lesion would abolish leftward gaze in both eyes. A frontal eye field lesion causes a conjugate gaze preference, not a dissociated failure of one eye.

quiz.question: A 10-year-old has a left third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil, a right hemiparesis, and a coarse tremor of the right hand that worsens as it reaches for a target. Which structure, beyond those of Weber syndrome, explains the tremor?
options: The red nucleus and the cerebellar outflow passing through it
The left medial lemniscus
The right cerebellar hemisphere
The left substantia nigra
quiz.explanation: A third-nerve palsy with opposite hemiparesis is the midbrain; adding an opposite-side tremor with ataxia means the lesion has reached the tegmentum, where the cerebellar outflow passes through the red nucleus after crossing. That is Benedikt syndrome (Pearl 2014, p. 110). The medial lemniscus carries sensation and would not cause a tremor. A right cerebellar lesion would cause right-sided ataxia but not a left third-nerve palsy. A nigral lesion causes slowness and rest tremor, not an action tremor with ataxia.

quiz.question: Which nystagmus in a dizzy 13-year-old should most change your plan from reassurance to an urgent brain MRI?
options: Horizontal-torsional nystagmus beating to the left that settles when she fixes on a target
A few beats of nystagmus at the extreme of lateral gaze
Pure downbeating nystagmus in primary gaze
Nystagmus that appears a few seconds after a positional manoeuvre and then fatigues
quiz.explanation: Pure vertical nystagmus is central and should send you looking for a brainstem or cerebellar lesion. Unidirectional horizontal-torsional nystagmus suppressed by fixation is the peripheral pattern. A few beats at the extreme of gaze is physiological end-point nystagmus. Delayed, fatiguing nystagmus after a positional manoeuvre is the peripheral positional pattern (Pearl 2014, pp. 120-121). Remember, too, that some antiseizure drugs cause a central-looking nystagmus, so the medication list belongs in the history.

quiz.question: A lesion destroys the left trochlear nucleus in the midbrain. Which superior oblique is weak, and why does this matter for the rule of four?
options: The left, because all medial motor nuclei serve their own side
Neither, because the fourth nerve is purely sensory
Both, because the trochlear nuclei are fused in the midline
The right, because the fourth-nerve fibres cross before they exit; it is one of the rule's exceptions
quiz.explanation: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve whose fibres cross completely before leaving the brainstem, and it leaves from the back. A nuclear lesion therefore weakens the opposite superior oblique, which breaks the rule that motor cranial nerve findings sit on the side of the lesion. Assuming same-side weakness is the error the rule would lead you into. The fourth nerve is motor, not sensory, and its nuclei are paired, not fused.
